Question: A good agent trace lets you answer:
Option A: Which step first departed from the gold policy, with the exact arguments and observation
Option B: Only whether the user clicked like
Option C: Only total GPU hours for the company

Question: A human-in-the-loop approval node is a state-machine feature. Skipping it in a free-form agent typically happens because:
Option A: The model can call the side-effecting tool directly if that tool is in scope
Option B: Graphs magically wrap every tool

Question: A retry storm from an agent usually looks like:
Option A: Many identical side-effecting calls after a slow 500, multiplying load and duplicate actions
Option B: A single well-bounded backoff
Option C: A user-visible stop after N errors
Option D: Jittered exponential backoff with a cap

Question: A token budget on an agent run should include:
Option A: System, history, each tool observation, and all model outputs—not only the last answer
Option B: Only the user’s first sentence

Question: A tool schema mismatch (string vs array) should be handled by:
Option A: Rejecting before execution, returning a structured error the model can repair, counting against the retry budget
Option B: Executing anyway and hoping
Option C: Raising temperature and resending to the tool
Option D: Dropping traces of the bad call

Question: A “search_files(glob)” tool plus “write_file(path, contents)” together are over-permissioned if the product only needs:
Option A: Read a ticket and post a comment
Option B: Full repository maintenance
Option C: A migration agent with human approval already in front
Option D: A coding agent in an isolated VM you accept

Question: An agent retries a 'create charge' tool on timeout. The first call may have succeeded. What do you need?
Option A: More retries; timeouts mean the charge did not happen.
Option B: Idempotency keys / a ledger you check before charging; retries of side-effecting tools are duplicates waiting to happen.
Option D: The model remembers the first charge in weights.

Question: Free-form looping is a poor fit when:
Option A: Compliance requires that refunds never precede identity verification, no matter what the model wants
Option B: The user is exploring an unknown codebase
Option C: Tool order cannot be known in advance
Option D: You are prototyping a research assistant

Question: In a tool loop, the model’s “plan” is only as good as:
Option A: The observation it actually received; a truncated or lying tool result will steer the next call
Option B: The parameter count of the base model alone
Option C: The absence of a stop token

Question: Parallel tool calls help latency but complicate retries because:
Option A: Partial success: some calls commit, others fail; you need per-call status, not one big undo
Option B: Parallelism forbids schemas
Option D: Traces cannot record more than one span

Question: Scratchpad vs retrieved semantic memory: which statement is right?
Option A: Scratchpad is in-run working notes; semantic memory is an external store you query. Mixing them without a write policy causes stale or leaked state
Option B: They are the same tensor
Option C: Scratchpad survives process death by default

Question: Tool timeouts should be:
Option A: Shorter than the remaining run budget, with a defined cancel/idempotency story
Option B: Infinite so the agent never fails
Option C: Hidden from the model so it assumes success

Question: Two agents share a scratchpad in natural language as their only memory. Why does this rot?
Option A: Natural language cannot represent tasks.
Option B: There is no schema, no conflict resolution, and no compact state — they overwrite, hallucinate prior steps, and diverge. Prefer structured state.
Option C: Scratchpads are encrypted and cannot be shared.
Option D: You need at least 12 agents for memory to work.

Question: When is “just add memory” the wrong fix?
Option A: The failure is a missing tool permission or a bad policy, and extra history only gives the model more ways to repeat it
Option B: The user refers to something said two turns ago inside the window
Option C: You retrieve the correct profile field
Option D: You store an audit log for humans

Question: You can replace a free-form agent with a state machine that still calls an LLM at specific nodes. When is that the better architecture?
Option A: Never; it reduces intelligence.
Option B: When most transitions are known and you want to constrain tools per state (support, KYC, deploy pipelines).
Option C: Only when the LLM is offline.

Question: You log thoughts in traces. A privacy issue is:
Option A: Thoughts and tool args can contain user secrets and must have retention and access controls like other prod logs
Option B: Traces cannot contain text
Option C: Thoughts are always synthetic and non-sensitive

Question: You should replace an agent with a compiled workflow when you notice:
Option A: The same two or three tool sequences succeed almost always
Option B: Every ticket needs a unique research path

Question: A 'manifest.json' object listing parts is a common S3 pattern because:
Option A: S3 cannot store more than one object
Option B: The bucket is not an index; you explicitly store the catalog you would have queried in a database

Question: A Lambda lists a prefix, then processes each key. The prefix has 5 million objects. Why does this design collapse?
Option A: LIST is strongly consistent but returns at most 1 key.
Option B: LIST is paginated and expensive; it is not a work queue. Use a manifest, S3 Inventory, or an event (SQS) per object.
Option D: S3 LIST locks the prefix, so only one Lambda can run.

Question: A Lambda processes SQS and writes S3. The Lambda times out after the PUT but before delete. What happens?
Option A: Exactly-once; SQS will not redeliver
Option B: The message returns after visibility timeout; you may PUT again — object writes and queue acks need idempotency keys

Question: A data lake on S3 plus Athena/Spark works when the object layout is:
Option A: One tiny file per event in a single hot prefix
Option B: Partitioned, reasonably sized files (columnar) so listing and scan costs stay bounded

Question: CloudFront in front of S3 helps popular reads. Origin load still spikes when:
Option A: Checksums are enabled
Option B: Cache misses, low TTL, or a unique-key stampede all go to the same prefix/object

Question: DLQs exist on SQS because at-least-once plus poison messages would otherwise:
Option A: Make S3 eventually consistent
Option B: Retry forever, blocking the queue; you isolate failures without pretending delivery was exactly-once

Question: FIFO SQS gives ordering per message group and exactly-once processing attempts inside a window, but you still:
Option A: Skip idempotency forever
Option B: Design consumers for retries, replays, and downstream side effects that may run more than once

Question: If-Match / If-None-Match on S3 give you optimistic concurrency for one key. They do not give you:
Option A: A way to avoid clobbering a single object
Option B: Multi-key transactions like a database

Question: Lifecycle transitions to colder storage classes are about access shape. A bad fit is:
Option A: Objects you rarely read
Option B: Objects you mutate or read with tight latency all day — retrieval cost and delay dominate

Question: Multipart upload is for large objects. Incomplete parts become a cost leak unless you:
Option A: Use sequential date prefixes
Option B: Abort abandoned uploads and set a lifecycle rule on incomplete parts

Question: Request costs for 1 billion 1KB objects vs one 1GB object differ because:
Option A: Durability percentages change
Option B: PUT/GET/LIST are billed per request; tiny objects turn storage into an API-tax problem

Question: S3 Event Notifications to SQS can fire more than once for the same object change. Downstream must:
Option A: Treat notifications as exactly-once ledger entries
Option B: Dedupe on object key + version/etag and stay idempotent

Question: S3 Select / Glacier select still does not replace a warehouse when:
Option A: Objects are larger than 400KB
Option B: You need repeated ad-hoc joins, mutating indexes, and concurrent transactional updates

Question: SQS delivers the same message twice to two consumers. What must your consumer assume?
Option A: Duplicates are a bug; open a ticket instead of making work idempotent.
Option B: At-least-once delivery: make the handler idempotent (dedupe key, conditional write) or you double-charge/double-apply.
Option C: SQS is exactly-once if you use long polling.
Option D: FIFO queues never redeliver after a visibility timeout.

Question: Storing session state only in S3 for a low-latency API is usually wrong because:
Option A: S3 cannot be private
Option B: Object GET/PUT latency and no cheap mutate path lose to an in-memory or purpose-built session store

Question: Versioning helps durability and recovery. It does not help you if:
Option A: You overwrite by mistake and want the old bytes
Option B: You needed a queryable current-row store; versions are extra objects, not an OLTP log you can SQL
Option D: You want to retrieve a prior checksummed copy

Question: You version objects and overwrite a key 1 million times a day. What cost/ops surprise hits later?
Option A: Versions are free and hidden.
Option B: Every overwrite keeps a full previous object (until you expire versions); list/delete/lifecycle work and storage grow without bound.
Option C: S3 coalesces versions into a delta log automatically.
Option D: Versioning only stores metadata, never bytes.

Question: A B-tree checkpoint/WAL design vs LSM WAL: what is the conceptual difference for user writes?
Option A: B-tree WAL protects in-place page mutations; LSM WAL protects memtable contents until flush
Option B: Only LSM uses a WAL
Option D: Neither needs a WAL if fsync is used on data files

Question: A B-tree update in place looks cheaper than LSM for a single row. When does the B-tree lose?
Option A: Never; in-place updates are always fewer bytes to disk.
Option B: When the working set of dirty pages is larger than cache and writes become random I/O across the tree.
Option D: When the table has no WAL.

Question: A B-tree update of a 100-byte row that lives in a 16 KiB leaf: what is the first-order write-amplification story?
Option A: You write ~100 bytes because only the row changes
Option B: You typically rewrite the whole leaf (and maybe ancestors on split), so amplification is page-sized not row-sized
Option C: Write amplification is always 1 because of WAL grouping
Option D: Only the bloom filter page is rewritten

Question: A workload is update-heavy on a small key set. Which engine property should you worry about first for LSM?
Option A: B-tree leaf splits
Option B: Compaction must keep rewriting those hot keys, so write amplification and tombstone/version churn stay high

Question: A write stall in an LSM engine is most often a symptom of what imbalance?
Option A: Bloom filters are too accurate
Option B: Flush/compaction cannot keep up with ingest, so memtables or L0 files pile up and writes are throttled
Option C: The WAL is too small to hold one record

Question: During an LSM range scan, bloom filters usually help how much?
Option A: They eliminate almost all SSTables, same as a point get
Option B: Little or none: a range may overlap many files, so you still merge-sort those overlapping runs
Option C: They convert the scan into a hash lookup
Option D: They replace the need for a block index

Question: Leveled compaction vs size-tiered: which statement about amplification is the useful default intuition?
Option A: Leveled usually trades higher write amplification for lower read and space amplification
Option B: Size-tiered always has both lower write and lower read amplification
Option D: The two strategies have identical amplification; only file names differ

Question: Range scans on an LSM often pull from several levels. What extra mechanism still helps point lookups more than ranges?
Option A: Bloom filters, which do not apply cleanly to arbitrary ranges.
Option B: The WAL, which is sorted by key.
Option C: Prefix compression, which makes ranges O(1).
Option D: Memtable skip lists, which replace SSTables for scans.

Question: Space amplification in LSM is high when…
Option A: Obsolete versions and overlapping runs have not been compacted away yet
Option B: Bloom filters use a few bits per key

Question: Why can a B-tree still beat LSM on a point get even when LSM has bloom filters?
Option A: A well-cached B-tree often needs one leaf I/O (plus a few internal nodes), while LSM may still miss cache on several files
Option B: B-trees never touch disk

Question: Why does a leveled LSM often bound point-read I/O to roughly one file per level (plus L0)?
Option A: Each level (except L0) keeps key ranges mostly non-overlapping
Option B: Only one SSTable exists in the whole tree
Option C: Bloom filters store the level number of every key
Option D: The memtable is searched instead of disk

Question: Why is WAL + memtable not enough by itself for long-term LSM health?
Option A: The WAL already stores sorted SSTables
Option B: Without flush and compaction, recovery time, file count, and obsolete versions grow without bound
Option C: Memtables cannot hold more than one key
Option D: Bloom filters cannot be built from SSTables

Question: Write amplification in an LSM is high. Compaction is always running. What is the engine spending I/O on?
Option A: Rewriting the same keys into new sorted runs as they age through levels, plus dropping tombstones.
Option B: Updating B-tree leaf pointers on every write.
Option C: Rebuilding Bloom filters for the WAL.
Option D: fsync of the memtable on every GET.

Question: You flush tiny memtables very frequently. What is the likely first-order effect?
Option A: Lower write amplification because files are small
Option B: Many overlapping SSTables, worse read amplification, and more compaction work later
Option D: Range scans no longer need merge iterators

Question: You need both fast random writes and efficient large range scans. What is the honest tradeoff to explain?
Option A: LSM favors ingest; scans pay merge cost across runs. B-trees favor locality; ingest pays random page writes
Option B: One structure always wins both, so pick either
Option C: Bloom filters make LSM scans as cheap as B-tree scans
Option D: Compaction removes the need to think about scans

Question: You undersize bloom filters so the false-positive rate is high. What happens to LSM point-read amplification?
Option A: Nothing; bloom filters are only used in compaction
Option B: More SSTables are opened and their indexes probed even though the key is absent

Question: A `std::function` callback captures `this` and is stored after the object dies. What is the failure?
Option A: std::function extends the object's lifetime.
Option B: A dangling `this`; the callback is a use-after-free when invoked. Own the callback lifetime or capture what you need by value.
Option D: The compiler rejects storing such functions.

Question: A data race on a non-atomic int is 'just a torn read' — why is that the wrong mental model in C++?
Option A: Data races are defined to return the last write.
Option B: A data race is undefined behavior: the compiler may miscompile the surrounding code, not merely tear the int.
Option C: The memory model only applies to atomics, so racy ints are always fine.
Option D: POSIX threads make all ints atomic.

Question: A template is defined only in a .cpp file. Other TUs that use it fail to link. Why?
Option A: Templates cannot be in cpp files ever.
Option B: The compiler needs the definition visible at instantiation, or you must explicit-instantiate; otherwise the linker cannot find the specialization.
Option C: You forgot `export template` which C++20 always requires.
Option D: The ODR allows one cpp to serve all TUs automatically.

Question: Exception from a destructor during stack unwinding. What does the language do?
Option A: It nested-catches the new exception.
Option B: If a destructor throws while another exception is in flight, the process calls std::terminate.
Option C: Destructors cannot throw by language rule, so this is a compile error.
Option D: The original exception is replaced silently.

Question: You need a concurrent queue. Rolling your own with one mutex is 'too slow', so you write a lock-free queue. What should you fear first?
Option A: Lock-free is always faster and easier to prove.
Option B: ABA, memory-order mistakes, and UB that only reproduces on the other CPU; a mutex queue is often the right first product.
Option C: mutex is illegal on more than two threads.
Option D: The standard provides a portable lock-free queue you must use.

Question: You pass a `std::initializer_list` that you stored for later. Why can it dangle?
Option A: initializer_list is a pair of pointers into a temporary array whose lifetime is the full expression.
Option B: initializer_list owns a vector.
Option C: It is a container like vector and is safe to store.
Option D: The backing array is in static storage.

Question: You return a `std::vector` by value. Why is that usually the right API in modern C++?
Option A: It always heap-allocates twice; callers should pass an output pointer.
Option B: NRVO/move make it cheap; returning by value states ownership clearly vs a raw pointer.
Option D: Return-by-value copies every time before C++23 only.

Question: shared_ptr copies in a tight loop show up in profiles. What are you paying for?
Option A: A mutex on every dereference of `*ptr`.
Option B: Atomic refcount updates and an extra control-block allocation; unique_ptr or a borrowed raw/span would avoid it when sharing is not required.
Option D: shared_ptr copies are free after inlining.

Question: A coordinator stores many hints for a down replica. What operational risk follows?
Option A: Hints improve read latency forever
Option B: Hint replay can storm the recovering node, and hints can expire so divergence remains until repair
Option C: The down replica is removed from RF automatically

Question: A partition for one customer grew to tens of GB. Queries to that customer are slow even at CL=ONE. What is the structural problem?
Option A: CL=ONE cannot read large partitions; you must use ALL.
Option B: The whole partition is the unit of co-location; one huge partition is a single-node hotspot and a wide-row read tax.
Option C: Cassandra automatically splits partitions at 100 MB, so this cannot happen.
Option D: Large partitions are stored in S3 and each read is a restore.

Question: A query with no restriction on partition key but a clustering-column filter is slow. Why?
Option A: Clustering filters require LWT
Option B: Without a partition key, Cassandra cannot target a replica set; it must scatter or reject/filter broadly
Option C: Bloom filters only work on clustering columns
Option D: QUORUM cannot be used without clustering columns

Question: An LSM-style memtable flush in Cassandra is most analogous to which cost you already pay in the storage engine?
Option A: Token hashing
Option B: Write path is fast sequential; later compaction and many SSTables create read amplification for that partition

Question: For RF=3, why is write QUORUM + read QUORUM the classic 'strong enough' pairing?
Option A: It contacts every node in the cluster
Option B: W+R>RF so the read set and write set must overlap on at least one replica

Question: LOCAL_QUORUM vs QUORUM in a multi-DC cluster: what did you change?
Option A: RF in every DC
Option B: You wait for a majority in the local DC only, not a cluster-wide majority, cutting cross-DC latency

Question: LWT on a hot partition is especially painful because…
Option A: Paxos storage is on a different cluster
Option B: Each LWT serializes competing proposers on that partition; hot keys queue behind in-progress rounds

Question: Range deletes and TTL expiry create many tombstones. Which read is most likely to time out?
Option A: A point get of a live key in a tiny partition with no deletes
Option B: A slice scan that must walk and skip huge runs of tombstones before finding live rows

Question: Read repair vs full/incremental anti-entropy repair: how should you think about them?
Option A: They are identical background jobs
Option B: Read repair may fix replicas touched by a query; anti-entropy repair walks token ranges to reconcile even cold data
Option D: Anti-entropy repair only runs on the coordinator's memtable

Question: Repair has not run for longer than gc_grace_seconds after many deletes. What resurrection bug are you exposed to?
Option A: Tombstones expired while a replica still has the old data; repair can copy the old row back.
Option B: Hinted handoff deletes all tombstones cluster-wide.
Option C: gc_grace only affects TTL columns, not DELETE.
Option D: Repair refuses to run if tombstones expired.

Question: Why can hinted handoff not replace repair?
Option A: Hints only cover some missed writes for a limited window; they do not reconcile all replica divergence
Option B: Hints always corrupt data
Option C: Repair cannot run if hints exist

Question: Why does Cassandra still need gc_grace-style delay before dropping tombstones?
Option A: To keep bloom filters warm
Option B: A replica that was down could otherwise resurrect deleted data after tombstones are gone
Option C: QUORUM counts tombstones as live votes

Question: Why is 'RF=3, CL=QUORUM, but NetworkTopologyStrategy with RF=3 in only one DC' a different failure domain than two DCs of RF=3?
Option A: It is not; RF is global
Option B: Quorum is computed from the keyspace's replica placement; one DC of 3 means a DC outage loses quorum, unlike per-DC RF=3 with LOCAL_QUORUM

Question: You model 'all events for a user' as partition=user_id, clustering=time. What hot-partition pattern should you expect?
Option A: Users are perfectly balanced by definition
Option B: Celebrity/hot users concentrate writes and reads on one partition and its replica set
Option C: Clustering by time spreads data across all tokens

Question: You write QUORUM and read ONE. What consistency property did you give up?
Option A: Durability of the commit log
Option B: The guarantee that the read intersects the write quorum; you can read a stale replica

Question: You write QUORUM and read QUORUM with RF=3. Why is this still not a linearizable compare-and-set for two clients updating the same cell?
Option A: QUORUM already provides linearizability for all writes.
Option B: Last-write-wins timestamps can still lose an update; you need LWT/Paxos (or an external consensus) for a true CAS.
Option C: QUORUM reads always see the latest write if the clocks are NTP-synced.
Option D: Cassandra serializes all writes to a partition through a single leader like Raft.

Question: A UI table sorts by selected column. Rows with equal values jump around every click. Users complain. Fix?
Option A: Use a stable sort, or add a hidden unique tie-breaker (original index) so the order is deterministic
Option B: Switch from array to linked list of rows
Option D: Put rows in a Bloom filter

Question: A priority queue of tasks also needs 'cancel task by id.' Plain binary heap problem?
Option A: Find-by-id is not a heap operation — keep a hash from id → heap index (or a tree of tasks) so decrease-key/delete is possible
Option B: Heaps already index by arbitrary id
Option C: Cancel is a BFS of the heap array
Option D: Use a Bloom filter as the heap

Question: An LRU cache is a hash map plus a doubly linked list. Why both?
Option A: The list gives O(1) lookup; the map gives recency.
Option B: The map finds the node in O(1); the list moves that node to most-recent in O(1) and evicts the tail in O(1).
Option C: The map is only for persistence; LRU can be a list alone in O(1).
Option D: A heap would be strictly better for LRU.

Question: Bloom filter at 1% false positive, you then always fetch the DB on 'yes.' What did you actually save?
Option A: Negative lookups skip the DB; positives (true and false) still pay the DB round trip — win is skewed to mostly-miss workloads
Option B: You saved the DB on all yes answers
Option D: The filter replaces the DB for yes and no

Question: Cache with consistent hashing. Client hashes to node A; A misses and fills from DB. Node A is added/removed and the key now lives on B, which is empty. User-visible issue?
Option A: Those keys thundering-herd the DB until B fills — consistent hashing reduces movement but does not zero it; replicas/shadow fills exist for that
Option B: Consistent hashing forbids misses after a membership change
Option C: LRU on B automatically contains A's memory

Question: Consistent hashing without virtual nodes, 3 physical caches of unequal capacity. Typical pain?
Option A: Arc sizes are lumpy — one node owns a huge key range; virtual nodes (many labels per physical) smooth load
Option B: All keys hash to node 0 by definition
Option C: Union-find is required to split the ring
Option D: LRU cannot run on a ring

Question: Consistent hashing without virtual nodes: one cache host dies. Why is the remap worse than it should be?
Option A: All keys must move to a random new host, not just the dead one's.
Option B: Only the dead node's keys should move, but without virtual nodes load was already skewed and neighbors absorb a huge slice.
Option C: Consistent hashing requires a coordinator to rewrite every key.
Option D: Dead nodes keep their keys until a full rehash.

Question: Graph of a social network: find people within 2 hops. Why BFS beats DFS here?
Option A: You care about distance layers; BFS emits level 1 then 2 and can stop. DFS can wander to hop 40 before it has finished hop 2
Option B: DFS cannot mark visited nodes
Option D: Heaps compute hop count faster than queues

Question: Hash table vs balanced tree for a language runtime dictionary. Hash is faster on average. When do you still pick the tree?
Option A: You need worst-case bounds, ordered iteration, or keys that are expensive/adversarial to hash — trees give comparable keys an order hash does not
Option B: Trees always beat hashes on point lookup
Option D: Linked lists iterate faster than both

Question: Kruskal-style clustering: merge closest pairs until k clusters. Why union-find instead of rerunning DFS?
Option A: Each merge and 'same cluster?' is cheap with disjoint sets; DFS from scratch every edge is repeating connectivity work
Option B: DFS cannot detect connected components
Option C: Heaps find components faster than union-find
Option D: Bloom filters cluster by hash collisions on purpose

Question: Online connectivity: unions arrive, and you also need the size of each component. Union-find tweak?
Option A: Store subtree/component size on the root; union by size and add sizes on merge — queries read the root's size after find
Option B: Run BFS from every node after each union
Option C: Put components in a max-heap keyed by an arbitrary id

Question: Workload: 10M keys, need 'all keys between A and B' and occasional insert. Engineer proposes a hash map. What fails?
Option A: Hashes do not keep order — range scan becomes a full table scan; an ordered tree (or B-tree / LSM with keys in order) matches the scan
Option B: Hash maps cannot insert after construction
Option D: A heap can range-scan in sorted order without extra cost

Question: You implement LRU with a hash map plus singly linked list. Evict-the-tail is easy; a hit in the middle is not O(1). Missing piece?
Option A: You need a back pointer (doubly linked) or an explicit prev in the map so you can unlink in O(1)
Option B: Singly linked lists are always O(1) to move a middle node
Option C: A Bloom filter of the tail replaces the list
Option D: BFS from the head on each hit is the standard LRU

Question: You must sort 1e8 records that are already almost sorted by timestamp, and equal timestamps must not reorder events. Which concern dominates?
Option A: Stability (and preferably an algorithm that is fast on nearly-ordered input) — a random-swap unstable sort both scrambles ties and fights the existing order
Option B: Only whether the textbook name is merge sort
Option C: Converting to a linked list first for locality
Option D: Inserting into a Bloom filter then iterating it

Question: You need a set-membership check in a scraper: 'have I already queued this URL?' Memory is tight, duplicates are annoying but not fatal. Structure?
Option A: Bloom filter (accept some extra fetches) — a hash set of all URLs may not fit; a tree of URLs is even heavier
Option B: A heap of URLs ordered by length
Option C: DFS stack as the only store
Option D: Union-find on characters of the URL

Question: You need the smallest k items from a huge stream. Why a size-k heap instead of sorting everything?
Option A: Heap of k gives O(n log k) extra memory O(k); full sort is O(n log n) and needs the whole set.
Option B: Sorting is O(n) and always better.
Option C: Heaps cannot compare items that arrive over a stream.
Option D: You must store all n items in the heap anyway.

Question: You store a graph as adjacency lists of linked nodes, then BFS a high-degree vertex. Hardware issue?
Option A: The neighbor list itself pointer-chases; a compact CSR/adjacency array scans neighbors in cache-line bursts and BFS gets faster without changing the algorithm
Option B: BFS is impossible without linked lists
Option C: DFS requires arrays; BFS requires lists

Question: A GSI has a partition key with much lower cardinality than the base table. Traffic looks fine on the table and throttles on the GSI. Why?
Option A: GSIs share the base table's partitions, so this cannot happen.
Option B: Each GSI is its own partitioned table with its own hot-key limits; a low-cardinality GSI key concentrates writes.
Option C: GSIs are eventually consistent, which is reported as throttling.
Option D: You must provision GSIs in RCUs only; WCUs do not apply.

Question: A GSI uses email as its partition key. Some emails are extremely popular write targets. What happens?
Option A: Only the base table can throttle; GSIs share infinite capacity
Option B: The GSI can hot-partition and backpressure base-table writes that must update that index

Question: A Query without a partition key is invalid because:
Option A: Query is just a slower Scan
Option B: Query is defined as 'read this partition (and maybe a sort-key slice)', not 'search the table'
Option C: Partition keys are optional on tables

Question: A reporting job Scans nightly 'because it is off-peak'. Why can this still hurt production?
Option A: Scans take a global lock
Option B: Scan still consumes read capacity and can steal throughput from live partitions if not isolated (separate table/export/on-demand job design)
Option C: Scans convert the table to provisioned

Question: A session blob is approaching a few hundred KB and is read on every API call. Best modeling move?
Option A: Keep growing the item; 400KB is a soft guideline
Option B: Move the blob to object storage and keep a pointer plus small, frequently read fields in DynamoDB
Option C: Store the blob as the partition key
Option D: Use Scan to fetch only one attribute

Question: Condition checks (optimistic locking with a version attribute) exist because:
Option A: PutItem always appends
Option B: Two writers can overwrite the same item; you need a predicate so the second write fails instead of clobbering
Option D: Strongly consistent reads lock the item

Question: Each order item also updates two GSIs. Under a write-heavy workload this matters because:
Option A: GSIs are read-only
Option B: Every base write fans out extra index writes, so write amplification and index hot keys become the limiter
Option C: GSIs batch all writes into one WCU
Option D: Index writes are free if the table is on-demand

Question: Item size is approaching hundreds of KB with a frequently updated counter inside the same item. What modeling pressure are you ignoring?
Option A: There is no write amplification; DynamoDB patches one attribute in place.
Option B: A write rewrites the whole item; fat items plus hot attributes waste WCU and increase conflict/latency. Split immutable blob from the hot counter.
Option C: Counters must live in S3 because DynamoDB cannot increment.

Question: Burstable pod: request 100Mi, limit 1Gi. Node memory pressure hits. Who dies first among BestEffort / Burstable / Guaranteed?

Question: A UUID PK was replaced by a sequential bigint PK, with UUID moved to a unique secondary index. What improved, and what remains?

Question: A locking range scan on a non-unique secondary index under RR deadlocks with inserts. What is a typical lock pattern?

Question: INSTANT ADD COLUMN succeeds on the source but an older replica breaks. What is the operational lesson?

Question: MIXED binlog format logs some statements as STATEMENT and some as ROW. When is MIXED still dangerous?

Question: Online ALTER adding a secondary index still causes replication lag. Why?

Question: Online DDL on a busy table still causes a latency spike. Which hidden cost is most often the real one?

Question: Parallel replica workers (logical clock / WRITESET) still serialize on one table. Why?

Question: Statement-based binlog plus a non-deterministic `UPDATE ... ORDER BY RAND() LIMIT 1` is replicated. What goes wrong?

Question: You chose a random UUID as the InnoDB primary key for a huge table. Why do writes get worse over time?

Question: You switch binlog_format to ROW to make replicas match. Which source-side cost appears?

Question: innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 2 improves COMMIT latency. What durability did you give up?

Question: A GIN index on jsonb speeds @> queries but INSERTs and VACUUM become expensive. Why?
